final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

comments.body:
Done with all the research. Summary:

1. **Hire vs DIY:** Hybrid — nothing described (barking, pulling, no lunging/biting) needs a full behaviorist, but a rescue + adolescent border collie is worth 2-3 professional sessions to get technique right, then you run it yourself.

2. **Trainers (South Bay = SF Bay Area assumption — please confirm, flag if you meant LA's South Bay instead):**
   - In Tune Dog Training (Nancy Le, San Jose): $150/90-min consult, force-free, rescue-experienced — cheapest starting point. Weekend availability is limited, though.
   - Off Leash K9 San Jose: ~$1,200 for an 8-lesson reactivity package, but uses e-collar/tool-based methods.
   - D For Dogz (Kaajal Tiwary): $2,400/6wk coaching or $4,200/6wk day-training — most structured, positive-reinforcement, has Sunday hours.

3. **4-week plan:** Week 1 management/foundations at home, Week 2 loose-leash mechanics + finding her "safe distance," Week 3 shrinking distance + pattern games on real routes, Week 4 consolidation + a progress check to decide whether to keep going solo or book more sessions. Full detail in the report.

Left one subtask for you: confirm the South Bay location assumption and call your preferred trainer to book. Everything else is done — parent task is `waiting` on that one human step.

report.markdown:
# Training Plan: 14-Month Rescue Border Collie Mix (Leash Pulling + Dog-Directed Barking)

**Location assumption:** "South Bay" was researched as the SF Bay Area / Silicon Valley (San Jose, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Mountain View, Cupertino, Campbell, Los Gatos, Milpitas, Palo Alto). If you meant South Bay Los Angeles (Torrance/Redondo Beach/Manhattan Beach area), the trainer options below don't apply — flag this and I can redo that part.

---

## 1. Hire a trainer, or do it yourself?

**Recommendation: Hybrid.** Do the day-to-day repetitions yourself, but pay for 2–3 professional sessions (or one evaluation + a reactive-dog class) up front.

Why not pure DIY:
- She's a rescue with an unknown history, and border collies are a sensitive, high-drive breed — <cite index="5-1,5-3">this can lead to leash reactivity, excitability, or anxiety, and addressing it requires calm leadership, structured training, and gradual desensitization</cite>. Getting the mechanics wrong early can intensify the pattern.
- 14 months is adolescence, the window where reactivity habits solidify if handled inconsistently.

Why not a full board-and-train or expensive extended program:
- Nothing in the description (barking, pulling) indicates lunging, biting, or fear/aggression — the threshold most professional guidance treats as requiring a behaviorist rather than a trainer-assisted DIY plan. General guidance is to <cite index="5-9">use a qualified trainer or veterinary behavior professional when safety, bite risk, or severe panic enter the picture</cite> — none of which is described here.
- Reactivity of this kind is very commonly resolved with structured owner-led work: <cite index="4-1,4-2">keeping the dog at a safe distance from other dogs so it doesn't need to practise barking and lunging is how desensitization and counter-conditioning work</cite>, and <cite index="2-13,2-14,2-15">keeping a loose leash, using gentle direction changes, and rewarding calm eye contact and neutral responses</cite> are all teachable skills.

**Bottom line:** book a session or two to (a) rule out anything beyond typical adolescent reactivity, and (b) get hands-on coaching on leash mechanics and threshold distance — then run the plan below yourself.

---

## 2. Trainer options (South Bay, CA — SF Bay Area)

| Trainer | Approach | Price | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **In Tune Dog Training** — Nancy Le, San Jose | Force-free / reward-based; CTC-certified (Academy for Dog Trainers honors grad); experienced with fearful/reactive rescues | **$150** for 90-min consult + management plan (Thurs/Fri only); ongoing session rate not published, ask directly | Covers Campbell, Sunnyvale, Cupertino, Santa Clara, Mountain View, Los Gatos, Milpitas, Los Altos. **Only "limited weekend availability"** — confirm this works with your schedule before booking. Contact via intunedogtraining.com |
| **Off Leash K9 Training of San Jose** | National franchise; has a dedicated 8-lesson "Reactive Dog" package (obedience + reactivity work) | First lesson **$500** (includes e-collar + 20-ft leash); each additional lesson **$100** → full 8-lesson package ≈ **$1,200** | Covers San Jose, Campbell, Saratoga, Los Gatos, Milpitas, Cupertino, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Mountain View, Los Altos. **Uses e-collar/tool-based ("balanced") training** — different philosophy than the other two; ask whether the e-collar is mandatory for a non-aggressive pulling/barking case. |
| **D For Dogz** — Kaajal Tiwary, San Jose | Positive reinforcement; dedicated "Leash Reactive Dog Foundations Program" with post-program support community | Private Coaching (you handle, trainer coaches): **$2,400/6 weeks**. Day Training (trainer handles dog directly): **$4,200/6 weeks** | Covers San Jose, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Cupertino, Mountain View, Campbell, Los Gatos, Milpitas, Los Altos, Palo Alto, Menlo Park, Atherton. Free 15-min phone consult. Hours Mon–Fri 9–7, **Sun 9–3** (your weekend slot). Phone: 650-538-3011. |

**Suggested path:** Start with **In Tune's $150 consult** — cheapest entry, force-free, specifically experienced with rescues — to get a professional read and coaching on technique. If more structured ongoing support is wanted afterward, **D For Dogz's Private Coaching ($2,400/6wk)** is the best-matched dedicated reactivity program; Off Leash K9 is the budget middle option but check your comfort with their e-collar-based method first.

---

## 3. Week-by-week plan (Weeks 1–4)

Built around evening (10–15 min) and weekend (longer walk-session) availability. Runs in parallel with whichever trainer sessions you book — trainer feedback should adjust real-time, but the structure below holds either way.

### Week 1 — Foundations & management (no real-walk drilling yet)
- **Goal:** Set up equipment and engagement, avoid rehearsing the reactive pattern while you build tools.
- **Gear:** Front-clip harness or head halter (reduces pulling leverage) instead of flat collar/back-clip.
- **Daily (evenings, 10–15 min, at home/yard):** "Name game" (say name, reward instant eye contact); hand-target training; short "find it" scatter-feeding for calm settling.
- **Weekend:** Walk at off-peak times/quieter routes specifically to avoid other dogs — this is management, not failure. Book/attend the trainer consult this week.
- **Management rule for all 4 weeks:** if you see a dog approaching and can't maintain distance, calmly u-turn or cross the street rather than let her rehearse barking — <cite index="4-3,4-4">keep her away from other dogs and ensure she doesn't meet any suddenly, staying at a distance where she feels secure</cite>.

### Week 2 — Loose-leash mechanics + sub-threshold distance work
- **Goal:** Teach loose-leash walking in a low-distraction environment, then find her "safe distance" from other dogs.
- **Daily (evenings):** Practice loose-leash in driveway/quiet street — stop walking the instant leash tightens, resume only when slack returns; reward position at your side.
- **Weekend:** Find a spot with dogs at a distance (far side of a large park, parking lot) where she notices but doesn't react — reward calm looking/disengagement at that distance. <cite index="2-22,2-23">Use calm exposure to triggers at safe distances — the goal is to make you more interesting than the trigger.</cite>
- Incorporate any corrections from trainer session 1 into your leash-handling.

### Week 3 — Shrinking distance + pattern games on real routes
- **Goal:** Gradually decrease distance to other dogs while maintaining calm; move drills onto your actual walking routes.
- **Daily (evenings):** Add pattern games — e.g., 1-2-3 stepping cadence, U-turn game — so she has a predictable job to focus on near triggers. <cite index="2-20,2-21">Use heel drills to keep her tuned in during movement and pattern games like 1-2-3 walking to reduce stress through predictability.</cite>
- **Weekend:** Longer walks incorporating 1–2 planned, controlled dog sightings at her working distance from Week 2, gradually a bit closer if she stays under threshold (no barking).
- Second trainer session (if using a package) should focus here on real-world troubleshooting.

### Week 4 — Consolidation + progress check
- **Goal:** Test generalization on regular routes and decide next steps.
- **Daily (evenings):** Continue loose-leash + engagement reps on normal routes.
- **Weekend:** Attempt closer, controlled passes with a known calm dog (arranged with a friend/neighbor) at a distance that's now easier than Week 1; keep sessions short and end on success.
- **Review:** Compare a short video from Week 1 vs. Week 4 walk. If clear improvement — continue DIY with occasional trainer check-ins. If little change or any escalation (lunging, increased intensity) — book additional structured sessions (D For Dogz coaching package or a reactive-dog group class) rather than continuing solo.

**General principles running through all 4 weeks:**
- <cite index="2-18,2-19">You can't train reactivity away with punishment — but you can replace it with engagement; a focused dog is a calm dog.</cite>
- Consistency matters more than session length — short daily reps at home plus the weekend real-world walks is the right cadence for an evenings/weekends schedule.
- <cite index="5-10">Keep the plan boring and consistent — dramatic corrections usually create more conflict than clarity.</cite>

---

subtasks.title: Decide: hire a trainer vs. DIY for leash pulling + dog-directed barking
subtasks.description:
Research whether a 14-month rescue border collie mix with leash pulling and barking/reactivity at other dogs on walks is realistically manageable with owner-led training, or whether professional help is recommended.

FINDING / RECOMMENDATION: Hybrid approach — do it yourself day-to-day, but pay for a handful of professional sessions to get the fundamentals right early.

Reasoning:
- Neither symptom described (pulling, barking) involves lunging, biting, or redirected aggression, which is the threshold most sources treat as a hard requirement for professional help. General guidance is to escalate to a trainer/behaviorist when there's bite risk, safety concern, fear/guarding, or repeated failed attempts.
- However, three factors argue for at least some paid professional input rather than pure DIY: (1) she's a rescue with unknown history/socialization, (2) border collies are a sensitive, high-drive breed where leash frustration reactivity can intensify if handled with the wrong technique (e.g., accidental punishment/flooding), and (3) 14 months is adolescence — the window where reactivity patterns solidify if not addressed correctly.
- Reactivity in border collies is very commonly described as manageable through structured, gradual desensitization and counter-conditioning (increasing distance from triggers, rewarding calm behavior, building engagement with the owner) — all things an owner can execute once shown the correct mechanics.

Practical recommendation: Book 2-3 private sessions (or one evaluation + a reactive-dog group class) with a force-free/positive-reinforcement trainer to (a) confirm there's no bite risk/fear-aggression requiring a behaviorist, (b) get hands-on coaching on loose-leash technique and threshold/counter-conditioning work for the barking, then run the day-to-day repetitions yourself using the 4-week plan. This is cheaper than a full board-and-train and puts the owner in the loop, which matters long-term for a working breed.

Find 2-3 trainers in the South Bay (assumed SF Bay Area / Silicon Valley: San Jose, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Mountain View, Cupertino, Campbell, Los Gatos, Milpitas, Palo Alto — NOT LA's South Bay; flag if wrong) who handle leash reactivity and dog-directed barking, with real prices.

THREE OPTIONS FOUND:

1) D For Dogz / Kaajal Tiwary (San Jose, serves San Jose, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Cupertino, Mountain View, Campbell, Los Gatos, Milpitas, Los Altos, Palo Alto, Menlo Park, Atherton) — positive reinforcement, has a dedicated "Leash Reactive Dog Foundations Program."
   - Private Coaching (you do the handling, trainer coaches you): $2,400 / 6 weeks, weekly sessions in your neighborhood + 90-min initial consult + between-session support.
   - Day Training (trainer works dog directly, you join every 3rd session): $4,200/6 weeks (or less if bundled - site mentions "save $420" enrolling full program).
   - Free 15-min phone consult available. Hours: Mon-Fri 9-7, Sun 9-3 (Sunday = your weekend slot). Phone: 650-538-3011.
   - Source: https://dfordogtraining.com/private-dog-training-silicon-valley/leash-reactive-dog-private-training/

2) In Tune Dog Training / Nancy Le (San Jose, 15-mile radius of Rose Garden neighborhood — covers Campbell, Sunnyvale, Cupertino, Santa Clara, Mountain View, Los Gatos, Milpitas, Los Altos) — force-free/reward-based, CTC-certified (Academy for Dog Trainers honors grad), experienced with fear/reactivity/aggression in rescues.
   - 90-minute Consultation Appointment: $150 (offered Thurs/Fri only), includes observation and a management plan.
   - Ongoing 1:1 weekly session pricing not published; needs a direct quote.
   - Availability is Mon-Fri with only "limited weekend availability" — a scheduling constraint given your evenings/weekends-only availability; ask when calling.
   - Source: https://www.intunedogtraining.com/training , https://www.intunedogtraining.com/contact

3) Off Leash K9 Training of San Jose (part of a national franchise, covers San Jose, Campbell, Saratoga, Los Gatos, Milpitas, Cupertino, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Mountain View, Los Altos) — has a specific 8-lesson "Reactive Dog" program bundling basic obedience + reactivity work.
   - First individual lesson: $500 (includes an e-collar and 20-ft leash provided as training tools).
   - Each additional lesson: $100/session (so an 8-lesson reactivity package ≈ $500 + 7×$100 = $1,200).
   - NOTE: this method uses e-collar/balanced training tools, not purely force-free — different philosophy than the other two options; worth asking directly whether e-collar use is mandatory or optional for a barking/pulling (non-aggressive) case.
   - Source: https://dogtrainerssanjose.com/prices/

SUMMARY TABLE (approx cost for a first round of help):
- In Tune (Nancy Le): $150 consult, then per-session TBD — cheapest entry point, force-free, best fit if you mainly want an evaluation + coaching on your own DIY plan.
- Off Leash K9: ~$1,200 for 8-lesson reactivity package — mid-price, but uses e-collar/tool-based method.
- D For Dogz: $2,400 (coaching) or $4,200 (day training) for 6 weeks — priciest but the most structured, dedicated reactive-dog program with ongoing community support.

Recommendation given the "hire a few sessions, then DIY" decision: start with In Tune Dog Training's $150 consult (cheapest, force-free, rescue-experienced) to get a professional read on the dog and technique coaching; use D For Dogz's private coaching as the fallback if more structured/longer support is wanted.

subtasks.title: Draft week-by-week training plan for first 4 weeks
subtasks.description:
Draft a week-by-week plan (Weeks 1-4) for loose-leash walking and reduced barking/reactivity to other dogs, built for evening/weekend sessions.

PLAN WRITTEN — see attached report on parent task t-dog for the full week-by-week breakdown. Core structure:
- Week 1: Management + foundations at home/yard (no-pull gear, engagement/"name game", find-it scatter feeding) — no real-walk reactivity drills yet, book trainer consult.
- Week 2: Loose-leash mechanics in low-distraction locations (quiet street/driveway) + start sub-threshold distance work with other dogs (parking lot, far side of a park).
- Week 3: Shorten distance to triggers gradually, introduce pattern games (1-2-3 walking, U-turns) on real walking routes, incorporate trainer feedback from session 1-2.
- Week 4: Consolidate on regular walking routes, test closer passes with known calm dogs, review progress against baseline (video weeks 1 vs 4) and decide whether to continue DIY or book more trainer sessions.

Each week is described with a specific evening/weekend session cadence (short daily 10-15 min home reps + 2-3 longer weekend walk sessions) since that matches the stated availability.
